## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Chores**
  * Minimum Node.js requirement raised to 26
  * CI/CD workflows and GitHub Actions updated to newer major versions
  * Docker base images updated to Node.js 26
  * Build/packaging now computes and validates certain dependency versions at build time
  * Documentation updated to reflect Node.js 26

* **New Features**
  * Startup logging added to indicate the chosen States DB (in-memory vs LMDB)

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Walkthrough

This PR upgrades the project to Node.js 26.x across CI workflows, Docker images, README, and package.json, and updates many GitHub Actions to newer major versions. It updates Docker-related workflow actions, adjusts Dockerfile base images to node:26, and raises engines.node to >=26. The build script now resolves several native dependency versions at build time and writes them into the generated package.json. LMDB configuration was changed so useWritemap honors the ephemeral flag, and importer logic centralizes and logs the selected States DB backend.

## Estimated code review effort

🎯 3 (Moderate) | ⏱️ ~20 minutes

- [FluffyLabs/typeberry#673](https://github.com/FluffyLabs/typeberry/pull/673): Related workflow changes for the vectors-update automation (GitHub App token and PR creation actions).
- [FluffyLabs/typeberry#981](https://github.com/FluffyLabs/typeberry/pull/981): Related LMDB configuration changes affecting write-map behavior in packages/jam/database-lmdb/root.ts.
- [FluffyLabs/typeberry#922](https://github.com/FluffyLabs/typeberry/pull/922): Also bumps Node.js and GitHub Actions/tooling versions across workflows and build artifacts.

actions/create-github-app-token@v3 Inputs: permission-* (granular permission scopes) - The action accepts optional permission inputs prefixed with permission- (e.g., permission-pull-requests). If you set a permission, the GitHub App installation must already have that permission; otherwise the action errors. [1][2] - Each permission-* input controls the level of permission granted to the resulting token (typically read or write; some support admin depending on the permission). [3][1] Input scope: repository targeting (where the token is scoped) - The token’s repository scope depends on owner and repositories inputs: - If neither owner nor repositories is set, access is scoped to the current repository. [4] - If owner is set and repositories is empty, access is scoped to all repositories in the provided owner’s installation. [4] - If repositories is set (with or without owner), repositories scopes the token to those repositories. [1][4] Outputs (what the action returns) - token: “GitHub installation access token” (an installation access token generated for the selected installation/permissions). [3][5] - installation-id: GitHub App installation ID. [3][5] - app-slug: GitHub App slug. [3][5] How the token is created (ties permissions + scope to the output) - The action creates an installation access token via POST /app/installations/{installation_id}/access_tokens. [5] - By default, the token inherits all permissions from the installation; if permission-* inputs are specified, the token is granted those specific permissions. [1][5] Note: token lifetime/revocation - Unless skip-token-revoke is set to true, the token is revoked in the action’s post step (so it can’t be passed to another job). [1][4]

🌐 Web query:

`GitHub Actions security best practice pin actions to commit SHAs mutable tags v6 v3`

💡 Result:

Best practice: Pin GitHub Actions (the `uses:` references) to full-length commit SHAs, not mutable tags like `@v6` or `@v3`. 1) Why tags like `v6` / `v3` are risky GitHub’s security guidance states that pinning to a full-length commit SHA is the only way to consume an action as an immutable release, and that pinning to a tag is risky because the tag can be moved or deleted by a bad actor (or if the action repo is compromised) [1]. 2) What to do instead (commit SHA pinning) - Replace `uses: OWNER/REPO@v6` (or any other `@v3`-style tag) with `uses: OWNER/REPO@<full-commit-SHA>`. - Optionally keep the human-readable tag as a comment next to the SHA. Example pattern shown in security/hardening guidance: `uses: actions/checkout@<full-SHA> # v4.0.0` [2]. 3) Enforce it (policy) GitHub supports policies that require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA. GitHub describes this as an organization- and repository-level mechanism, where workflows using unpinned actions fail [1]. GitHub’s changelog also notes administrators can enforce SHA pinning so workflows using actions that aren’t pinned fail [3]. 4) Practical maintenance Pinning requires maintenance when you want updates, but you can automate updating the pinned SHAs using tools/workflow rules (e.g., keep the SHA pins current while retaining immutability) [2]. Bottom line Do: `uses: some-action@<full-commit-SHA>` Don’t: `uses: some-action@v6` or `uses: some-action@v3` (or any other mutable tag), unless you fully trust the action creators and accept the risk that the tag reference can be altered [1].

- 1: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use
- 2: https://architecture.lullabot.com/adr/20260505-pin-github-actions-to-hash/
- 3: https://github.blog/changelog/2025-08-15-github-actions-policy-now-supports-blocking-and-sha-pinning-actions/

The `actions/create-github-app-token` action (v3) allows you to generate a GitHub App installation access token within a workflow [1][2][3]. Permissions Input To grant specific permissions to the generated token, use the `permission-` prefix followed by the permission name (e.g., `permission-pull-requests: write`) [1][2][4]. By default, the token inherits all permissions granted to the GitHub App installation [1][2][3]. It is recommended to explicitly list required permissions to follow the principle of least privilege [1][2]. Note that if you request a permission that the installation does not possess, the action will return an error [1][2][4]. Scope Inputs The token's scope is determined by the `owner` and `repositories` inputs: - Default: If no target inputs are provided, the token is scoped to the current repository [1][2][3]. - `repositories`: If specified, the token is scoped to those repositories [1][2][4]. - `owner` (without `repositories`): The token is scoped to all repositories within the specified owner's installation [1][2][4]. - `enterprise`: Creates a token for an enterprise installation [1][4]. Output The primary output is: - `token`: The generated GitHub installation access token [5][2][3]. Additional outputs include: - `installation-id`: The ID of the GitHub App installation used [5][2]. - `app-slug`: The slug of the GitHub App [5]. The generated token is automatically masked to prevent accidental logging and is, by default, revoked in the action's `post` step once the job completes (unless `skip-token-revoke` is set to `true`) [1][2][3].

[1] GitHub also notes that even though using tags is convenient, tags can be moved or deleted by an attacker, so there’s inherent risk even if you trust the action’s creators. [3] Note: This best practice applies to all actions you use (and often also actions referenced inside other actions). If your organization enables SHA-pinning enforcement, any tag-based reference anywhere in the dependency tree can cause failures. [4]

It is highly recommended to explicitly limit permissions to the minimum required for your specific use case [1][7][3]. - Constraints: You can only grant permissions that have already been granted to the GitHub App installation itself; requesting a permission not held by the installation will result in an error [1][2][6]. - Repository Scoping: If you provide the `repositories` input, the token is scoped only to those specified repositories [3][5]. The `actions/create-github-app-token@v3` action allows you to generate a GitHub App installation access token with granular, restricted permissions [1][2]. By default, a token generated by this action inherits all permissions granted to the GitHub App installation [1][3]. However, it is highly recommended to use the `permission-` inputs to restrict the token to only the permissions necessary for your specific workflow [4]. To restrict permissions, you can use the `permission-` prefix followed by the permission name as a key in the `with` block [4]. The values can be set to `read`, `write`, or other levels appropriate for the specific permission [5][4]. For the specific permissions you mentioned, you can configure them as follows [5]: - permission-contents: Can be set to 'read' or 'write' to manage repository contents [5]. - permission-pull-requests: Can be set to 'read' or 'write' for pull requests, comments, assignees, labels, milestones, and merges [5]. Example configuration: ```yaml - uses: actions/create-github-app-token@v3 id: app-token with: app-id: ${{ vars.APP_ID }} private-key: ${{ secrets.PRIVATE_KEY }} permission-contents: write permission-pull-requests: write ``` Important Notes: 1. Prerequisites: The GitHub App must already have these permissions granted at the installation level [4]. If you specify a permission that the installation does not possess, the action will return an error [4]. 2. Security: This approach follows the principle of least privilege, mirroring the recommendation to control permissions for the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` [4]. 3. Revocation: Unless `skip-token-revoke` is set to `true`, the token is automatically revoked in the post-step of the action [1][3].
